faqs.q: I found a raccoon in my Beaufort attic — can you move it to the woods?
faqs.a: South Carolina law does not work that way. SCDNR states that routine relocation of wildlife is against state law, and an animal captured near a home must be destroyed or, only with a separate department permit, may be relocated. In Beaufort we solve it with eviction and exclusion instead: a one-way door lets the raccoon leave the attic on its own, or the animal is removed under SCDNR depredation rules, and then every entry around historic district's raised antebellum homes housing is sealed in steel. Raccoons are the top rabies carrier in SC Department of Public Health testing, so droppings and latrine areas are cleaned and sanitized as part of the job.

faqs.q: There is an alligator in our Beaufort pond. Can you remove it?
faqs.a: No — and be wary of anyone in South Carolina who offers that as a routine service. Alligators are state-listed as Threatened here and are handled only through SCDNR's program: nuisance alligators are reported to SCDNR, which issues tags and permits to property owners or sends a contracted Alligator Control Agent. What we can do in Beaufort is the safety side: keep people and pets back from pond edges near historic district's raised antebellum homes, never feed an alligator, and call SCDNR promptly if one is acting as a nuisance.

faqs.q: What does a wildlife removal job in Beaufort actually involve?
faqs.a: It starts with the inspection, and the scope grows or shrinks with what that inspection finds around historic district's raised antebellum homes: how many entry points the animal has opened, whether young are present, and how much exclusion the roofline and crawlspace need. A single squirrel entry sealed in a day is a small job; a raccoon family with latrine cleanup and a full roofline seal is a larger one. We walk you through each item we find before the work is set, so the scope you approve is the scope we do.

Season decides the timing, especially when litters or bat pups mean part of the work waits a few weeks. You get the full picture from the inspection before committing to the plan.

faqs.q: Are armadillos really established around Hilton Head Island?
faqs.a: Yes. Nine-banded armadillos are established throughout the entirety of South Carolina, and around here they burrow under porches, driveways, and crawlspace edges and root up lawns hunting grubs and worms. We trap the animals working your property and backfill and screen the burrow openings, because an open burrow in this soil is quickly claimed by the next armadillo — or by a skunk or opossum.

faqs.q: There is a dead animal smell in my Hilton Head Island walls. What should I do?
faqs.a: Call us rather than opening walls at random. Our crew locates the carcass — a dead raccoon, opossum, or squirrel in a wall void or crawlspace is the usual source — removes it, and sanitizes the area. Carcasses of raccoons, skunks, and bats are handled with rabies precautions in line with Department of Public Health guidance, and we check how the animal got in so the entry is sealed as part of the same visit.

faqs.q: An alligator has taken up in the lagoon behind our Hilton Head home. Can you remove it?
faqs.a: No — and be wary of anyone who offers. Nuisance alligators in South Carolina are handled only through SCDNR, which assigns its contracted hunters; private operators have no authority to trap or move one, and an alligator that is simply present in a lagoon is not classed as a nuisance at all. What we can do is assess your property honestly: most lagoon-side concerns are solved by distance and habit — no feeding ever, pets kept off the bank, and the yard side of the fence line managed. If an animal is genuinely aggressive or has lost its fear of people, we will tell you exactly how the SCDNR report works and what to expect from it.

faqs.q: Our Hilton Head villa is rented out and managed from out of state. How does the work get verified?
faqs.a: On paper, completely. We handle the gate access and community requirements with your manager, inspect the whole structure — roofline, fascia, under-deck voids, and the trash enclosure — and deliver a photographic record of every entry found and every seal made, with the depredation permit details for the property. Rental owners cannot walk the roofline; the report has to do it for them, and ours is written to that standard. It also becomes the document your manager holds if the problem ever becomes a neighbour's claim about whose raccoon it is.

Hilton Head Island.wildlife_intro:
Our crew works Hilton Head Island from the sea-pine and live-oak villa communities and lagoon systems. The homes here sit in sea islands, salt marsh, and live-oak maritime forest, with raised Lowcountry homes behind marsh and tidal creek, and that habitat explains most of what we find: raccoons, opossums, armadillos, gray squirrels account for the bulk of our Hilton Head Island calls, moving between the wild ground and the housing along the same creeks, field edges, and canopy streets every night.

Raised Lowcountry and antebellum homes on the islands, resort villas on Hilton Head, and fast-built subdivisions in Bluffton, many over crawlspaces in sandy soil. In spring we handle denning raccoons and squirrels before litters grow, in summer the calls shift to bats, skunks, and digging animals in the yards, and in fall we seal homes ahead of the winter push. Every Hilton Head Island job starts with a full inspection of the roofline, foundation, and crawlspace, and ends with the entries sealed — because in Beaufort County there is always another animal nearby ready to use an open hole.

Hilton Head is a planned island, and its planning is the wildlife story. The gated plantations were built inside the live oak and palmetto forest, around a system of lagoons that threads every community — so a Hilton Head home stands in managed habitat by design: canopy overhead, water in the back, and a standing population of raccoons, gray squirrels, opossums, and armadillos that treats the landscaping as infrastructure. Bats work the fascia of the older villas, roof rats run the palmettos in the denser villa communities, and the lagoon banks hold the island's famous alligators, which are scenery and law, not a removal service — an alligator that is genuinely a nuisance is SCDNR's call, through its contracted hunters, and anyone who tells you otherwise is improvising.

The part-time pattern doubles the pressure. A large share of Hilton Head homes are second homes and rentals, standing quiet between visits — and a quiet villa in the canopy is claimed the same way quiet houses are everywhere, except that here the claimant pool is an island's whole population with nowhere else to go. Our Hilton Head inspections are built for absent owners: whole-structure reads, gate-community logistics handled, and a photographic record of every entry and seal that an owner can verify from another state.
Hilton Head Island.extendedBody:
Lagoons, canopy, and the villa roofline

Hilton Head's entries follow its design. Palmettos and oaks bridge to the rooflines of the villas and single-family homes alike; the lagoon system puts raccoon traffic along every back lot line; and the older villa communities — the island's 1970s and 80s stock — carry fascia and soffit details at the age where bats and squirrels both prospect them. We seal in materials chosen for salt air and for the eye: in the plantations, how exclusion looks is part of whether it is allowed, and we spec to community standards as a matter of course. Gator safety shapes the lagoon-side work — no trapping programme runs a bank an alligator is using, and the schedule bends around the island's real residents without drama.

South Carolina rules, island edition

There is no SCDNR operator license — a referral list only. Removal on Hilton Head runs on the depredation permit for your property under §50-11-2570(A), with the state's rules attached: bats excluded by SCDNR's timing guidance, never sealed in while pups are flightless; rabies-suspect animals reported through SC DPH; and alligators entirely outside private removal — a nuisance gator is reported to SCDNR, which assigns its contracted hunters. Deer, the island's other famous population, are managed by the communities and the town, not by trappers. An operator who is clear about what is not theirs to do is usually clear about the rest.

Rentals and the turnover problem

Rental villas add a wrinkle: guests feed nothing intentionally, but a raccoon that has learned a villa's trash enclosure teaches the street. Our rental work weights the enclosures, the grill areas, and the under-deck voids alongside the roofline, and documents everything for the property manager — because in the rental market, the report is what the owner actually receives, and it has to be good enough to act on without a site visit.

faqs.q: We have rats in our Port Royal attic. How is that different from squirrels?
faqs.a: Rats work at night and squirrels work at dawn, which is the first clue. In Port Royal, roof rats climb from trees, vines, and utility lines around Battery Creek marsh, while Norway rats burrow along foundations and come up through plumbing gaps. We identify the species, trap inside the structure, and seal the entry points at roof and foundation level — poison alone leaves dead rats in walls and does nothing about the openings.

We clear the animals with one-way doors, seal the full roofline in metal, and point out the access routes worth trimming back.

faqs.q: Why do squirrels keep getting into Lady's Island attics?
faqs.a: Gray squirrels need an opening little more than an inch wide, and the usual doors here are soffit corners, gable vents, and the gaps where additions meet the main roof, reached from fences and overhanging limbs. Trapping without sealing just invites the next squirrel, so our crew fits one-way doors, lets the animals leave, and seals every opening in steel — timed so a nursing litter is never sealed inside.

faqs.a: Call us rather than opening walls at random. Our crew locates the carcass — a dead raccoon, opossum, or squirrel in a wall void or crawlspace is the usual source — removes it, and sanitizes the area. Carcasses of raccoons, skunks, and bats are handled with rabies precautions in line with Department of Public Health guidance, and we check how the animal got in so the entry is sealed as part of the same visit.

faqs.q: Raccoons keep getting under our Lady's Island deck from the marsh side. How do you close it for good?
faqs.a: By screening the void as a system, not patching the entry of the week. Marsh-side decks give raccoons a covered den with a feeding route attached — the creek bank — so we remove the residents, then screen the full deck perimeter with mesh buried at the base, because raccoons dig at edges and a surface-only screen is a curtain, not a wall. We also check the roofline above the same elevation: the animals using a deck void test the house it is attached to, and the visit that closes both ends the commute entirely.

In spring we handle denning raccoons and squirrels before litters grow, in summer the calls shift to bats, skunks, and digging animals in the yards, and in fall we seal homes ahead of the winter push. Lady's Island is Beaufort's mainland shore — the island across the bridges from the historic city, where live oak canopy, salt marsh, and tidal creek frontage wrap a fast-growing residential community. Its wildlife work is Lowcountry marsh work: raccoons commuting the creek banks and marsh edges into attics and under decks, opossums and armadillos in the sandy yards, bats in the older homes and over the marsh at dusk, and gray squirrels through the oak hammocks that shade most of its streets. Lady's Island never had a wild edge to lose; it is built inside the marsh system, and the marsh keeps its tenants.

The growth adds the second pattern: new subdivisions along the US-21 corridor and the island's interior, built into pine and oak woods, inherit the displaced pattern — first-year attics tested by raccoons, moles in new lawns, snakes along the fresh pond and marsh edges. Our Lady's Island inspections weight whichever pattern the address carries, marsh-edge or clearing-edge, and most addresses here carry some of both.
Lady's Island.extendedBody:
Creek banks, marsh edges, and the commute

Lady's Island's animal traffic runs on the water lines. Raccoons work the tidal creeks and marsh banks as feeding routes and take the houses along them as den sites — under the raised decks and porches especially, and into the attics of the older marsh-side homes. Our marsh-edge inspections include the bank side of the property: the deck voids, the dock structures, and the canopy contacts where the oaks bridge to the roof. Sealing a marsh-side house only at the front elevation is the classic local half-job; the animals arrive from the water side, and the water side is where the sealing has to be complete.

The permit framework in the Lowcountry

South Carolina issues no wildlife operator license — SCDNR keeps a referral list only. Our Lady's Island work runs on the depredation permit for your property under §50-11-2570(A), with the state's handling rules: bats excluded by SCDNR's timing guidance, never sealed in while pups are flightless; rabies-suspect animals reported through SC DPH; alligators — present in the island's creeks and ponds — outside private removal entirely, and referred to SCDNR when one is genuinely a nuisance. In marsh country the distinctions matter, and an operator who draws them clearly is telling you how the rest of the job will go.

Storm season and the tired roofline

Coastal storms write Lady's Island's entry list a season ahead: lifted fascia, torn screens, and soffits worked loose by one hurricane season are the next season's raccoon and bat entries, and marsh-side homes take weather the inland streets do not. A post-storm roofline check is the cheapest wildlife work on the island — the gaps a storm opens are precisely the gaps the creek-bank population patrols.
